title: Can you set a default time zone for the entire application (TimeZone.setDefault, spring.jackson.time-zone, DB session, Docker TZ)?
shortTitle: Setting a Default Time Zone for the Entire Application
keyPoints: A Java application's default time zone is resolved from several layers: JVM, serialization, database session, and OS/container.
The JVM time zone is set with -Duser.timezone=UTC or TimeZone.setDefault() once at startup.
Spring Boot's spring.jackson.time-zone=UTC makes Jackson serialize dates in that zone consistently.
The JDBC/Hibernate time zone (hibernate.jdbc.time_zone=UTC) ensures timestamps are read and written consistently.
The Docker TZ environment variable sets the container's zone, which the JVM inherits at startup.
Standardize all layers on UTC so behavior is deterministic across dev, test, and production environments.
Convert to the user's local zone only at the presentation edge using explicit ZonedDateTime.

s1_definition.oneliner: Yes: set a default time zone at the JVM, Jackson/JSON, database session, and OS/Docker layers, and standardize all of them on UTC so the whole application behaves deterministically everywhere.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **JVM timezone** – set with `-Duser.timezone=UTC` (preferred) or `TimeZone.setDefault(TimeZone.getTimeZone("UTC"))` once at startup.
- **Jackson timezone** – `spring.jackson.time-zone=UTC` makes JSON serialization consistent.
- **JDBC/Hibernate timezone** – `hibernate.jdbc.time_zone=UTC` so timestamp values are not silently shifted.
- **Docker/OS timezone** – `ENV TZ=UTC` in Dockerfile sets the container's zone, inherited by the JVM.
- **Best practice** – set all layers to UTC; convert to user's local zone only at the presentation edge.
- **Caution** – `TimeZone.setDefault()` affects the entire JVM process (all threads); set once at startup, never at runtime.
s1_definition.analogy: It is like the National Bank of India deciding that every clock in every branch, every form, and every computer runs on one agreed time standard. You can set that standard in several places: the building clock (OS/Docker), the staff handbook (JVM), the way reports are printed (JSON serialization), and the central ledger system (database). If you only set one and forget the others, different parts drift and disagree, so the right move is to set them all to the same standard: UTC.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Yes, you can and should set a default time zone for the whole application, but the important insight is that the "default" is resolved from several layers and they must agree. At the JVM level, set `-Duser.timezone=UTC` or call `TimeZone.setDefault()` once at startup. At the serialization layer, set `spring.jackson.time-zone=UTC`. At the database layer, set `hibernate.jdbc.time_zone=UTC`. At the container layer, set `ENV TZ=UTC` in the Dockerfile.

The crucial senior point is to set these consistently rather than piecemeal. The classic "works on my machine, wrong in production" time bug comes from the layers disagreeing. A service at the National Bank of India ran correctly in development where hosts were IST but produced timestamps shifted by 5.5 hours in a cloud region with a different host zone, precisely because it relied on the implicit host default. Pankaj fixed it by pinning UTC at all four layers and converting to IST only when rendering to users with explicit `ZonedDateTime`.

Modern code should prefer `java.time` types with explicit zones over leaning on any default. `TimeZone.setDefault()` affects the entire JVM process and every thread, so it must be set once at startup and never toggled at runtime. Store everything in UTC internally and convert to the user's local zone only at the presentation edge.

Remember one sentence: set a default time zone at the JVM, Jackson, database, and Docker layers and standardize all of them on UTC so the whole application behaves deterministically everywhere.
